newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian investment forum taps $786 million.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian investment forum taps $786 million.

text.p: Tanzania's first international investor forum ended on Friday with a preliminary signing of contracts worth at least $786 million.

"The biggest contracts were in build, operate and transfer, a petroleum pipeline, a hydro-electric dam plus one in mining which was huge also," said Thomas Abela, Africa regional coordinator for the U.N. Industrial Development Organisation.

Abela made the announcement at the end of the four-day investment and technology forum. More than 300 international investors and 150 Tanzanian investors met and discussed more than 160 projects, organisers said.
The biggest deal signed was a $400 million project to build a petroleum pipeline from Dar es Salaam to the strategic northern port of Mwanza on Lake Victoria.
Other major deals were a $43 million construction project for a hydro-electric dam and a $160 million mining sector deal to develop a mine in northern Bulyanhulu.

While participants hailed the success of the forum, warnings were given to the Tanzanian government to make good on its promises to slash red tape and bureaucracy seen as major impediments by potential investors.
In a welcoming speech on Tuesday, President Benjamin Mkapa promised to ease visa and work permit regulations for investors.

He said he would establish a task force to look at ways of streamlining Tanzania's complex taxation system which investors and even government officials see as a quagmire of ill-conceived legislation designed to strangle local business.
At a post-forum news conference, Trade Minister Abdallah Kigoda and Acting Finance Minister Daniel Yona reiterated the government's commitment to slash bureaucracy.

"Our aim is to have a small civil service which is professional, efficient, hard-working and well-paid. The reforms are not just on the economic front," Yona said. "This is a transition from an old (socialist) system to a new system. So, I think bureaucracy will disappear as we move along."
The forum resulted in the signing of four joint venture contracts and 75 letters of intent covering $786 million including 10 technology transfer projects valued at $3 million.

Other smaller deals involving Tanzania's embryonic manufacturing sector covered cotton ginning, gold refining, ceramic ware production, quarries, and production lines for nylon bags, domestic appliances and finished leather products.

"An analysis of the business meetings forms returned by participants showed that with few exceptions participants will continue negotiations towards investment decisions and project implementation. Letters of intent while less forceful are a measure of confidence," Abela said.
Tanzania's dilapidated infrastructure served as its own advertisement for foreign investors, said David Mwaibula, chairman of the chamber of commerce, industry and agriculture.

"I believe tourism, mining, infrastructure, non-working telephones, roads which are impassable -- all these are opportunities," he said to widespread laughter from the estimated 400 guests in the hotel ballroom.
